name: Rust
title: Rust from the first line
intro: Rust is a systems language in the same neighbourhood as C, with a compiler that refuses a large class of memory mistakes before the program ever runs. These lessons use the 2021 edition: printing, names, choices, loops and functions, then the rule that a value has one owner. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.rs and type rustc hello.rs && ./hello, or use cargo new for a project.

sections.p: A Rust program starts in fn main. println! prints a line. The ! means it is a macro, not an ordinary function: it checks the format string when the program is compiled. Text goes in double quotes.
{} is a hole in the string. Each value after the string fills the next hole. {:?} is the debugging form, useful for seeing exactly what a value is.

practice.why: println! prints the text and then ends the line. The quotes and the ! are not printed.
Each {} is replaced by the next argument, and the space between them is an ordinary character in the string.

practice.q: Why does println! end with an exclamation mark?
options: It is a macro, checked at compile time
practice.answer: It is a macro, checked at compile time
practice.why: The ! marks a macro. println! can reject a format string that does not match its arguments before the program runs.

practice.q: Where does a Rust program start?
practice.why: main is the entry point. println! only prints.
A line starting with // is a comment and never runs.

lessons.title: Names and mut
lessons.summary: let, and why the default is immutable.

sections.p: let gives a name to a value. By default the name cannot be pointed at a new value later. let mut allows that. Rust figures out the type from the value: 5 is an integer.
You can let the same name again. That is a new binding, not a change to the old one, so it is allowed even without mut. The new binding can even have a different type.

practice.why: mut allows the assignment. n becomes 10 − 3.

practice.q: Which line will the compiler reject?
practice.why: Without mut, a name cannot be assigned again. Shadowing with a second let is a different, legal, thing.
The second let hides the first. Its value is 2 * 5.

options: The name may be assigned a new value
The value is shared with other threads
practice.answer: The name may be assigned a new value
practice.why: mut means mutable. The default, without mut, is that the binding does not change.
a is still 1. b is a new name holding a + 1. Reading a does not use it up, because i32 is copied.

sections.p: if does not use brackets around the test. The branch is a block. == compares; = assigns, and an assignment is not a test.
A block can end in an expression with no semicolon, and that expression is the block's value. So if can be used on the right of let. Both branches must produce the same type.

practice.why: n == 2 is true, so only the first branch runs.
1 is not greater than 5, so the else expression is the value of the if.
== compares. = is assignment, and it is not allowed as the test of if.

practice.q: What must be true when if is used as a value?
options: Both branches produce the same type
practice.answer: Both branches produce the same type
practice.why: The if expression has one type. A branch that ends in a number and a branch that ends in text do not match.
4 fails the first test and passes the second. The else is not reached.

sections.p: for walks a range. 0..3 is 0, 1 and 2: the end is left out. 0..=3 includes 3. print! is println! without the newline. continue skips the rest of the current pass.
while repeats while a test is true. Something in the test has to change, or the loop does not end.

practice.why: 1..=3 includes 3. print! does not add a newline, so the digits sit on one line, and println!() ends it.
The body runs for n = 0 and n = 1. Then n is 2 and the test fails.
A range written with .. leaves out the end. ..= would include it.

practice.q: Why is n declared mut in the while example?
options: The loop assigns a new value to n
while requires mut on every name
n is shared with another thread
practice.answer: The loop assigns a new value to n
practice.why: n = n - 1 changes the binding, so it must be mut. The test reads n; reading alone would not need mut.
continue skips the rest of this pass. 2 is not printed, then the loop goes on to 3.

lessons.title: Functions and ownership
lessons.summary: Parameters, return values, and one owner.

sections.p: A function names its parameter types and, after ->, its return type. The last expression of the body, with no semicolon, is the value returned. A semicolon would turn it into a statement that returns nothing.

A String has one owner. Assigning it to another name moves it: the old name may no longer be used. Integers are Copy, so assigning an i32 copies it and both names stay usable. Passing &name lends a reference without moving the string.

practice.why: twice returns n * 2, and the call passes 4. The missing semicolon means that expression is the return value.

practice.q: Which function body returns the sum?
practice.why: An expression without a semicolon is the block's value. A semicolon throws the value away. println! prints but returns ().

practice.q: What happens to a String when you assign it to a new name?
options: It moves, and the old name can no longer be used
It is copied, like an i32
practice.answer: It moves, and the old name can no longer be used
practice.why: String is not Copy. The new name becomes the owner. An i32 is copied instead, which is why both names still work for numbers.

practice.q: What does &name pass to a function?
options: A borrow, leaving you as the owner
The string, which you then lose
practice.answer: A borrow, leaving you as the owner
practice.why: A reference lets the function look at the value without taking ownership.
A function with no -> returns (). Each call prints one line.

lessons.title: Borrowing and references
lessons.summary: Using a value without taking it.

sections.p: Passing a String to a function moves it, and the caller can't use it any more. Usually you only want to let the function look. Writing &name lends a reference, and the parameter type &String (or better, &str) says the function borrows. When the function returns, the loan ends and the owner carries on.
sections.out:
hazelnut has 8 letters
a literal works too: 5

sections.p: To let a function change a value, lend it with &mut. Rust's central rule is that at any moment you may have either any number of shared references or exactly one mutable one, never both. That rule, checked by the compiler, is what rules out data races and many of C's pointer bugs.

A slice borrows part of a collection: &v[1..3] is elements 1 and 2 of a vector, and &s[0..3] is the first three bytes of a string. A &str is a string slice. Functions that take slices work with whole collections and parts of them alike.

practice.why: Each call borrows s mutably and adds one character.
1..3 includes index 1 but not 3, so the slice is [20, 30].

practice.q: Which borrows can exist at the same time?
options: Many shared (&) references, or one mutable (&mut) reference
Only one reference of any kind
practice.answer: Many shared (&) references, or one mutable (&mut) reference
practice.why: Readers can share, but a writer needs exclusive access.

lessons.title: Structs and methods
lessons.summary: Your own types, with impl blocks.

sections.p: A struct groups named fields. Methods go in an impl block. A method's first parameter says how it uses the value: &self to read, &mut self to change it. A function in the block without self, such as new, is called with :: and is often used as a constructor.

#[derive(...)] asks the compiler to write common behaviour for you. Debug lets {:?} print the value, Clone adds .clone(), and PartialEq adds ==. Struct update syntax, ..other, fills the remaining fields from another value.

practice.why: Each tick adds one and returns the new count.

practice.q: What does &mut self in a method's parameters mean?
options: The method may change the value it is called on
The method takes ownership and destroys the value
practice.answer: The method may change the value it is called on
practice.why: &self reads, &mut self changes, and self (without &) takes ownership.

options: The ability to print the value with {:?}
practice.answer: The ability to print the value with {:?}
practice.why: The compiler writes the formatting code for every field.

lessons.title: Enums, match and Option
lessons.summary: A value that is one of several kinds.

sections.p: A Rust enum lists the kinds a value can be, and each kind can carry its own data. match picks code for each kind and pulls the data out. The compiler checks that every kind is handled, so adding a new one shows you every place that needs updating.
sections.out:
5 nuts
nothing today
12 sunflower seeds
a single nut

sections.p: Rust has no null. A value that may be missing has type Option<T>, an enum with two kinds: Some(value) or None. You can't use the value without handling None first, with match, if let, or a helper such as unwrap_or.
sections.out:
found beech
hazel has 5 letters
no tree
Some("OAK")

practice.why: a holds 4, so 4 * 2 = 8; b is None, so unwrap_or gives 7.
match is an expression; the Amber arm gives "wait".

practice.q: What happens if a match does not handle every kind of an enum?
practice.why: Matches must be exhaustive; _ can stand for all remaining kinds.

lessons.title: Errors with Result and ?
lessons.summary: Failures you have to deal with.

sections.p: Operations that can fail return Result<T, E>: Ok(value) on success or Err(error) on failure. Turning text into a number with parse is one. As with Option, the compiler makes you look at the result before using the value.
sections.out:
42 -> 42
forty-two -> error: invalid digit found in string
-3 -> error: invalid digit found in string

sections.p: Inside a function that itself returns Result, the ? operator means: if this is an Err, return it from the function now; otherwise take the value out and carry on. That keeps the happy path readable. You can define your own error type, often an enum, and map_err converts one error into another.

unwrap() takes the value out of an Ok or Some and panics, stopping the program, if there is none. expect("message") does the same with a clearer message. Use them in quick experiments and where failure would be a bug in your own code, and return a Result where the failure comes from outside, such as user input or a missing file.

practice.why: 12 halves to 6 and then to 3. 6 halves to 3, and halving 3 fails, so quarter returns that Err.

practice.q: What does ? do on an Err value?
options: Returns that error from the current function
practice.answer: Returns that error from the current function
practice.why: On Ok it unwraps the value; on Err it returns early.

practice.q: Where is unwrap() a reasonable choice?
options: In quick experiments, or where failure would be a bug in your own code
When opening files chosen by the user
practice.answer: In quick experiments, or where failure would be a bug in your own code
practice.why: For failures that come from outside, return a Result so the caller can decide.

lessons.title: Collections, iterators and closures
lessons.summary: Vec, HashMap, and chains of iterator methods.

sections.p: A closure is a function written in place: |n| n * 2. Iterators take closures in methods such as filter, map and sum. The chain does nothing until something consumes it, such as sum, count or collect, which builds a new collection.

HashMap stores values by key. entry(key).or_insert(0) gives a mutable reference to the value for a key, inserting 0 first if it is missing, which makes counting a one-liner. A hash map keeps no particular order, so copy the pairs into a Vec and sort them before printing.

String is growable, owned text; &str is borrowed text. Both are UTF-8, so len() counts bytes and chars() walks real characters. split_whitespace, to_uppercase, contains and format! cover most daily needs.
sections.out:
5 words, longest: squirrel
THE-SQUIRREL-BURIED-AN-ACORN
6 bytes, 5 chars
true

practice.why: The even numbers 2, 4 and 6 become 20, 40 and 60, which add up to 120.
"a" appears three times, and there are two different keys.

practice.q: When does a chain like v.iter().map(...).filter(...) do its work?
options: Only when something consumes it, such as sum, count or collect
As soon as map is called
Never; it must be in a for loop
practice.answer: Only when something consumes it, such as sum, count or collect
practice.why: Iterators are lazy, which also lets them stop early with take.

lessons.title: Traits and generics
lessons.summary: Shared behaviour, and code that works for many types.

sections.p: A trait names behaviour that types can share, like an interface in other languages. Each type implements it in an impl Trait for Type block. A trait can give a default method that types get for free. Implementing the standard Display trait lets a type be printed with {}.
sections.out:
tree hollow holds 120
burrow 30 cm deep holds 60
Burrow(30)

sections.p: A generic function such as fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy> works for any type with the listed traits; the compiler makes a fast copy for each type it is used with. When a collection must hold different types that share a trait, use a trait object, Box<dyn Store>, and the right method is chosen while the program runs.

practice.why: Sam only supplies name; hello comes from the trait's default.

practice.q: When do you need Box<dyn Trait> instead of a generic T: Trait?
options: When one collection must hold values of different types
practice.answer: When one collection must hold values of different types
practice.why: A Vec<T> holds one type; a Vec<Box<dyn Trait>> can mix any types that implement the trait.

practice.q: What does implementing fmt::Display for a type allow?
options: Printing it with {} in println! and format!
practice.answer: Printing it with {} in println! and format!
practice.why: {:?} needs Debug; {} needs Display.

lessons.title: Project: a nut ledger
lessons.summary: Structs, enums, Result, HashMap and iterators together.

sections.p: This program reads a small ledger written as text, one entry per line, such as day 3: acorn x9. It parses each line into a struct, collecting errors for bad lines instead of stopping, totals each kind of nut in a HashMap, and prints a sorted report. Notice how ? keeps the parser short, and how split_once returns an Option that ok_or turns into an error.
sections.out:
line 4 skipped: bad day: invalid digit found in string
line 7 skipped: missing ':'
acorn     15  68.2%
hazelnut   6  27.3%
walnut     1   4.5%
best find: 9 acorn on day 3

sections.p: Read the ledger from a file with std::fs::read_to_string (which returns a Result too), replace the String errors with an error enum, or add a Display implementation for Entry so it can print itself.

practice.why: split_once returns the parts before and after the first ": ", and the program prints them swapped.

practice.q: Why does the program collect errors per line instead of using ? in main?
options: So one bad line is reported and skipped instead of stopping the whole report
practice.answer: So one bad line is reported and skipped instead of stopping the whole report
practice.why: ? passes the error up; here main decides to log it and carry on.

options: Turns an Option into a Result, using the given error for None
Turns a Result into an Option
Returns true when the value is Some
practice.answer: Turns an Option into a Result, using the given error for None
practice.why: That lets ? be used on Options inside a function that returns Result.
